title: Game 5: Lasker–Capablanca
subtitle: A supported knight becomes the centre of the strategy

narration.say: Lasker has White against Capablanca at St. Petersburg in 1914. White exchanges the bishop for the knight.
The central exchanges bring an early queen trade. Black develops the bishop.
Both sides develop and castle. White advances f4.
The knight retreats to b3. Black supports the centre with f6.

steps.title: Space and the cost of a bishop exchange

narration.say: White advances f5 and develops the bishop. Black develops the other bishop to b7.
Capablanca criticises his bishop move. White exchanges on d6 and centralises the knight.
The pawn on f5 supports e6. White can place a knight deep in Black’s position.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Establish the knight on e6.

narration.say: White brings the rook to d1. Black retreats the knight, and White doubles rooks against d6.
White fixes the queenside and brings the king into play.
White gains kingside space while keeping pressure on d6.
The kings approach the critical area.

steps.title: Switch the rooks to the kingside

narration.say: White moves the rook across. Black checks with the g-pawn.
The pawn exchange opens the h-file. White brings one rook there, then doubles.

steps.title: Open the centre at the right moment

narration.say: The knight on e6 remains strongly supported. White now opens another route for the pieces.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Challenge the pawn on d6.

narration.say: The second knight centralises while the first jumps to c5.
White takes the rook on d7 and invades the seventh rank.
The other rook changes wings and checks from a8.
Black resigns. The active rooks and knight have overwhelmed the defence.

steps.title: An outpost is part of a whole plan

narration.say: The knight on e6 restricted Black and gave White time to improve rooks, pawns and king.
White attacked the centre and then switched to the h-file. The second knight joined at the decisive moment.
Do not judge an outpost only by its square. Ask how the rest of your pieces can exploit the opponent’s restrictions.
